enum: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / Not applicable (cross-sectional intercept survey and single-wave semi-structured interviews; survey refusal/non-response rates among approached spring users are unreported, though environmental loss of the JdF spring drying up in 2014 is noted)
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (exploratory descriptive MCA and qualitative case-study triangulation with no causal comparator design or multivariable adjustment for socioeconomic, demographic, or spatial confounders across neighbourhoods)
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate (accurately characterizes municipal statutory responsibility for sanitation/water quality, Queimados's 30-year concession contract delegating operations to state utility CEDAE, federal PAC pipeline investments, and non-institutionalized FUNASA/municipal spring monitoring via documents and official interviews, but lacks formal statutory citations or contract-clause coding)
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern (9-item survey was pre-tested in preliminary field visits, but water quality in the survey reflects subjective user perception—100% good-to-excellent despite external E. coli detection—and collection frequency/network status are self-reported; qualitative interviews used a 21-question protocol and inductive coding, but report no verbatim transcripts/quotes or inter-coder checks)
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate (captures spring usage type, collection frequency, household network/well access, and perceived water quality in an intercept sample of n=90, supplemented only by secondary municipal/FUNASA reference to a November 2013 Escherichia coli test rather than systematic microbiological or volumetric household measurement)
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern (no study protocol or pre-analysis plan; quantitative results are reported mainly as an MCA factorial map and aggregate percentages without neighbourhood-stratified contingency tables or item missingness, qualitative results omit direct interviewee quotes, and raw data are unavailable)
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern (non-probabilistic convenience intercept sample of 90 users collected over just 3 summer days across two weeks in Jan–Feb 2014 at 2 of 21–31 natural springs in Queimados, with unknown sampling fraction/refusal rate; purposive sample of 9 institutional and community interviewees)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S1: Are there clear research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper clearly states its exploratory objective to investigate how formal public water networks and informal grassroots spring solutions coexist ('spotted zebra' hybrid system) in Queimados (RJMR), examining users, water uses, stakeholder relations, vulnerabilities, and institutional barriers/drivers.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 1–3, 5–6 (Abstract; Introduction, pp. 188–189; Methodology, pp. 191–192)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S2: Do the collected data allow to address the research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Combining an on-site user survey at two contrasting natural springs (n=90), 9 in-depth semi-structured interviews with public officials, utility staff, and community actors, and documentary sources directly addresses the area, actors, and flows of the hybrid water system.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.1: Is the qualitative approach appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: An inductive qualitative case-study component using key-informant and stakeholder semi-structured interviews alongside documentary investigation is well suited to uncovering institutional arrangements, clientelist dynamics, and governance barriers in hybrid water provision.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 5–6, 12 (Methodology, pp. 191–192; Actors and flows, p. 198)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.2: Are the qualitative data collection methods adequate to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Fieldwork spanned one year, selecting 3 key informants based on Tremblay's (1982) criteria (FUNASA biologist, municipal environmental licensing director, Guandu River Basin Committee director) plus 6 additional interviewees (CEDAE commercial director and two local technicians, neighbourhood association leader, former vice-mayor, and spring caretaker), using a 21-question open protocol across 4 macro-themes.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 5–6, 12 (Methodology, pp. 191–192; Actors and flows, p. 198)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.3: Are the findings adequately derived from the data?
domain_ratings.justification: Recorded interviews were transcribed into text and systematically coded using Thomas's (2006) general inductive approach into 12 analytical categories via progressive filtration, then triangulated into four thematic dimensions (socio-cultural, health and vulnerability, politico-institutional, technical-infrastructural).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF p. 12 (Actors and flows; Triangulation, p. 198)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.4: Is the interpretation of results sufficiently substantiated by data?
domain_ratings.justification: Although findings attribute specific points to identifiable informant roles (e.g., FUNASA officer, Guandu Basin Committee director, former local administrator), the paper includes zero verbatim interview quotations and does not display the 12 analytical coding categories, preventing independent verification of how raw qualitative data support the narrative interpretations.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 12–15 (Findings: Actors and flows & Triangulation, pp. 198–201)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.5: Is there coherence between qualitative data sources, collection, analysis and interpretation?
domain_ratings.justification: There is clear conceptual and methodological coherence linking the socio-technical systems / co-production framework (Faldi et al., 2019), stakeholder selection, interview macro-questions, Thomas (2006) inductive coding, and the four-dimensional barrier/driver synthesis.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 5–6, 12–16 (Methodology, pp. 191–192; Findings & Conclusions, pp. 198–202)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.1: Is the sampling strategy relevant to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Purposively selecting two active springs representing contrasting infrastructural contexts—Jardim da Fonte (urbanized, piped network present) and Vila do Rosário (peri-urban, unserved by piped network)—and intercept-surveying users when no demographic census of spring users existed was pragmatically relevant for an exploratory descriptive profile.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.2: Is the sample representative of the target population?
domain_ratings.justification: The sample (n=90) is explicitly non-probabilistic and purposive, collected during only 3 days across two summer weeks (January–February 2014) at just 2 of the municipality's 21–31 springs, with no sample-size calculation, per-spring quota breakdown, or check of representativeness across seasons or other springs.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 6, 9 (Methodology, p. 192 & fn. 2; Informal water supply system, p. 195)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.3: Are the measurements appropriate?
domain_ratings.justification: The 9-question survey covered clear categorical indicators (household size, collection frequency, spring water uses, public network connection, well ownership, and perceived water quality) that were pre-tested during preliminary field visits and peer-briefed; authors appropriately distinguish subjective perceived water quality from microbiological potability.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.4: Is the risk of nonresponse bias low?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper provides no information on the total number of spring users approached during the three survey days, refusal/non-participation rates, or item-level missingness, making non-response bias impossible to verify.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 6, 9–11 (Methodology, p. 192; Findings: Area, pp. 195–197)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.5: Is the statistical analysis appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Summary proportions and Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA; Greenacre, 2010) are well suited to visualizing multivariate associations among categorical survey variables (explaining 75.69% of inertia across F1=70.64% and F2=5.05%), although underlying contingency tables by neighbourhood are omitted.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 6, 9–11 (Methodology, p. 192; Findings, Table 1 & Fig. 2, pp. 195–197)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.1: Is there an adequate rationale for using a mixed methods design to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: The mixed-methods design is explicitly justified via Faldi et al.'s (2019) three-dimensional hybrid-service framework: quantitative user surveying captures the 'area' dimension (users, resources, and water-use patterns) while qualitative interviews capture 'actors' and 'flows' (institutional responsibilities and socio-political relations), combined via Mathison (1988) triangulation.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.2: Are the different components of the study effectively integrated to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: A dedicated Triangulation section integrates MCA/survey patterns, stakeholder interview accounts, and institutional/water-quality records across four analytical dimensions rather than reporting the quantitative and qualitative strands in isolation.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.3: Are the outputs of the integration of qualitative and quantitative components adequately interpreted?
domain_ratings.justification: Integrated interpretation generates coherent socio-technical insights, showing how formal CEDAE network intermittency/absence drives differentiated spring reliance (drinking-only supplement in piped JdF vs all-purpose necessity in unpiped VdR) within an unaccountable institutional vacuum.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.4: Are divergences and inconsistencies between quantitative and qualitative results adequately addressed?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors explicitly confront divergences between survey perceptions and institutional/scientific evidence—specifically that 100% of surveyed users rated spring water quality positively (especially 'excellent' in JdF) whereas municipal/FUNASA interviews and a November 2013 microbiological test revealed Escherichia coli contamination and lack of potability guarantees—and also note the 67% male water-fetching share contrasting with standard Global South literature.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.5: Do the different components of the study adhere to the quality criteria of each tradition of the methods involved?
domain_ratings.justification: Under MMAT 2018 criteria, adherence is compromised by significant limitations in the quantitative descriptive strand (non-representative 3-day summer convenience sample of n=90 at only 2 springs [4.2 = No], unreported non-response rate [4.4 = Can't tell], missing subgroup frequency tables) and reporting gaps in the qualitative strand (absence of direct verbatim quotes and researcher reflexivity [1.4 = Can't tell]).

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Maiello, de Paiva Britto, and Quintslr (2021) present a convergent/triangulated mixed-methods case study of formal-informal hybrid water supply ('the spotted zebra') in Queimados, Rio de Janeiro Metropolitan Region. Appraised with MMAT (2018) using the Quantitative Descriptive block (4.1–4.5), the study's main strengths lie in its conceptual coherence and genuine mixed-methods integration (5.1–5.4 all Yes): the authors align a 90-respondent user survey (analysed with Multiple Correspondence Analysis) and 9 semi-structured stakeholder interviews (inductively coded following Thomas 2006) with Faldi et al.'s (2019) area-actors-flows framework, and effectively contrast subjective user perceptions (100% rating spring water good-to-excellent) against institutional testimonies and microbiological records showing Escherichia coli contamination and spring depletion. However, per MMAT 2018 guidance that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component, methodological concern is moderate-to-high (5.5 = No): the quantitative survey relies on a non-probabilistic convenience sample collected over just three summer days at 2 of the municipality's 21–31 springs (4.2 = No) with unreported refusal/non-response rates (4.4 = Can't tell) and no neighbourhood-stratified contingency tables, while the qualitative report provides zero verbatim interview quotations or researcher reflexivity discussion to substantiate its thematic coding (1.4 = Can't tell) and raw data are closed.
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate-to-high methodological concern (narrative MMAT judgment, no numeric score: strong mixed-methods rationale and triangulation [5.1–5.4 Yes], but bounded by non-representative 3-day convenience sampling [4.2 No], unreported survey non-response [4.4 Can't tell], and lack of verbatim qualitative quotes/reflexivity [1.4 Can't tell; 5.5 No])
raw_response.study_design_identified: Convergent/triangulated mixed-methods exploratory case study combining a cross-sectional quantitative descriptive user survey analysed with Multiple Correspondence Analysis (n=90 natural spring users) and qualitative semi-structured interviews (n=9 key informants and stakeholders) with documentary analysis
raw_response.where_found_summary: Methodology (PDF pp. 5–6 / pp. 191–192); Case study institutional background (PDF pp. 7–9 / pp. 193–195); Survey & MCA Findings, Table 1 and Fig. 2 (PDF pp. 9–12 / pp. 195–198); Semi-structured interviews & Triangulation across four dimensions (PDF pp. 12–15 / pp. 198–201); Data availability statement (PDF p. 17 / p. 203).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The paper reports primary empirical collection, analysis, and explicit triangulation of both quantitative data (a structured 9-question field survey of 90 spring users analysed statistically via Multiple Correspondence Analysis) and qualitative data (9 semi-structured interviews transcribed and inductively coded into 12 categories per Thomas 2006). Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, MMAT (2018) with the Quantitative Descriptive component (4.1–4.5) is the exact matching tool for a genuine mixed-methods primary study without an experimental/quasi-experimental comparator.
